Excerpt: This campaign comprises two distinct categories of victims: staging and intended targets. The initial victims are peripheral organizations such as trusted third party suppliers with less secure networks. The initial victims are referred to as “staging targets” throughout this alert. The threat actor uses the staging targets’ networks as pivot points and malware repositories when targeting their final intended victims. The ultimate objective of the cyber threat actors is to compromise organizational networks, which are referred throughout this alert as “intended target.” DHS leveraged the Cyber Kill Chain model to analyze, discuss, and dissect malicious cyber activity. Phases of the model include reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on the objective. This section will provide a high-level overview of activity within this framework. The threat actors appear to have deliberately chosen the organizations they targeted, rather than pursuing them as targets of opportunity. Staging targets held preexisting relationships with many of the intended targets. It is known that threat actors are actively accessing publicly available information hosted by organization-monitored networks. DHS further assesses that threat actors are seeking to identify information pertaining to network and organizational design, as well as control system capabilities, within organizations. Forensic analysis identified that threat actors are conducting open-source reconnaissance of their targets, gathering information posted on company-controlled websites. This is a common tactic for collecting the information needed for targeted spear-phishing attempts. In some cases, information posted to company websites, especially information that may appear to be innocuous, may contain operationally sensitive information. As an example, the threat actors downloaded a small photo from a publically accessible human resources page. The image, when expanded, was a high-resolution photo that displayed control systems equipment models and status information in the background.

The initial victims, known as "staging targets," are typically third-party suppliers with less robust security measures. These organizations serve as a launchpad for the threat actors to gain initial access to the networks of their final, more critical targets. The ultimate goal is to infiltrate the networks of key organizations, which are referred to as "intended targets." 

The analysis of this campaign was conducted using the Cyber Kill Chain model, which breaks down the lifecycle of a cyber attack into several phases: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on the objective. Threat actors appear to have meticulously selected their targets based on strategic considerations, rather than opportunistic choices. Many of the staging targets had pre-existing relationships with the intended targets, making them a convenient stepping stone.

DHS observed that the threat actors actively gather information from publicly available sources, including company-controlled websites, to understand the organizational and network design. This information is crucial for more sophisticated attacks, such as targeted spear-phishing campaigns. For instance, the threat actors exploited innocuous information posted on human resources pages, which, when magnified, revealed sensitive details about control system equipment and operational status.

This approach highlights the importance of maintaining strict control over sensitive information and the need for thorough cybersecurity measures to protect against such targeted attacks.

Excerpt: Analysis also revealed that the threat actors used compromised staging target networks to conduct open-source reconnaissance to identify potential targets of interest and intended targets. “Targets of interest” refers to organizations that DHS observed the threat actors showing an active interest in, but where no compromise was reported. Specifically, the threat actors accessed publically web-based remote access infrastructure such as websites, remote email access portals, and virtual private network (VPN) connections. Throughout the spear-phishing campaign, threat actors used email attachments to leverage legitimate Microsoft Office functions to retrieve a document from a remote server using the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. (An example of this request is: file[:]//<remote IP address>/Normal.dotm). As a part of the standard processes executed by Microsoft Word, this request authenticates the client with the server, sending the user’s credential hash to the remote server prior to retrieving the requested file. (Note: It is not necessary for the file to be retrieved for the transfer of credentials to occur.) The threat actors then likely used password-cracking techniques to obtain the plaintext password. Once actors obtain valid credentials, they are able to masquerade as authorized users. When seeking to compromise the target network, threat actors used a spear-phishing email campaign that differed from previously reported TTPs. The spear-phishing email used a generic contract agreement theme, with the subject line “AGREEMENT & Confidential”, and which contained a generic PDF document, titled “’’document.pdf”. (Note the inclusion of two single apostrophes at the beginning of the attachment name.) The PDF itself was not malicious and did not contain any active code. The document prompted the user to click on a link should a download not automatically begin. (Note: No code within the PDF initiated a download.) The link directs users to a website via a shortened URL, which may prompt them to retrieve a malicious file.

Our latest analysis reveals that the threat actors have been conducting a targeted reconnaissance campaign, leveraging compromised staging networks to identify and assess potential targets of interest. These targets, while not yet compromised, are of significant interest to the threat actors, as evidenced by their active surveillance. The reconnaissance involved accessing publicly available web-based remote access infrastructure, such as websites, remote email portals, and virtual private networks (VPNs), to gather intelligence.

The threat actors employed a sophisticated spear-phishing campaign that included the use of carefully crafted emails with a generic contract agreement theme. The subject line "AGREEMENT & Confidential" was designed to evoke curiosity and a sense of urgency. The email contained a PDF attachment with a misleading filename: “’’document.pdf”. (The inclusion of two single apostrophes at the beginning of the attachment name is intended to mislead recipients.) This PDF did not contain any malicious code, but it prompted users to click on a link if the download did not start automatically.

Excerpt: Network devices are ideal targets. Most or all organizational and customer traffic must traverse these critical devices. A malicious actor with presence on an organization’s gateway router has the ability to monitor, modify, and deny traffic to and from the organization. A malicious actor with presence on an organization’s internal routing and switching infrastructure can monitor, modify, and deny traffic to and from key hosts inside the network and leverage trust relationships to conduct lateral movement to other hosts. Organizations that use legacy, unencrypted protocols to manage hosts and services, make successful credential harvesting easy for these actors. An actor controlling a router between Industrial Control Systems – Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (ICS-SCADA) sensors and controllers in a critical infrastructure—such as the Energy Sector—can manipulate the messages, creating dangerous configurations that could lead to loss of service or physical destruction. Whoever controls the routing infrastructure of a network essentially controls the data flowing through the network. Russian state-sponsored cyber actors have conducted both broad-scale and targeted scanning of Internet address spaces. Such scanning allows these actors to identify enabled Internet-facing ports and services, conduct device fingerprinting, and discover vulnerable network infrastructure devices. Protocols targeted in this scanning include Login banners and other data collected from enabled services can reveal the make and model of the device and information about the organization for future engagement. Device configuration files extracted in previous operations can enhance the reconnaissance effort and allow these actors to refine their methodology. Commercial and government security organizations have identified specially crafted SNMP and SMI packets that trigger the scanned device to send its configuration file to a cyber-actor-controlled host via Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP), User Datagram Protocol (UDP) port 69. If the targeted network is blocking external SNMP at the network boundary, cyber actors spoof the source address of the SNMP UDP datagram as coming from inside the targeted network. The design of SMI (directors and clients) requires the director and clients to be on the same network. However, since SMI is an unauthenticated protocol, the source address for SMI is also susceptible to spoofing.
messages.output:
Network devices, such as routers and switches, are prime targets for malicious actors due to their critical role in managing and directing data traffic within an organization. By compromising these devices, attackers can monitor, modify, or even block traffic, thereby gaining significant control over the network's data flow. For instance, if a malicious actor gains access to an organization’s gateway router, they can intercept and manipulate data sent to and from the organization, putting sensitive information at risk. Similarly, an actor with access to the internal routing and switching infrastructure can monitor and manipulate traffic between key hosts, potentially using the established trust relationships to move laterally across the network.

Organizations that still rely on legacy, unsecured protocols for managing hosts and services make it easier for attackers to steal credentials. For example, an actor controlling a router in an Industrial Control System (ICS) environment, such as the Energy Sector, can tamper with communication between sensors and controllers. This manipulation could result in dangerous configurations that might lead to a service disruption or physical damage. Whoever controls the routing infrastructure essentially holds the key to managing data flow, making it a critical point of vulnerability.

Russian state-sponsored cyber actors have been known to conduct extensive scanning of Internet address spaces to identify and target vulnerable network infrastructure devices. This scanning helps them to pinpoint open ports and services, allowing them to gather device fingerprints and discover potential vulnerabilities. The protocols targeted in these scans include login banners and other data from enabled services, which can reveal the make and model of the devices and provide insights into the organization’s network architecture. Previously extracted device configuration files from prior operations can further refine their understanding and tactics.

Cyber actors often leverage specially crafted Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and Structured Management Information (SMI) packets to trigger the targeted device to send its configuration file via Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) over UDP port 69. Even if the network is configured to block external SNMP, actors can spoof the source address to bypass these restrictions. Since SMI is an unauthenticated protocol, the source address can be easily manipulated, making it a weak point in the security posture of the network.

Excerpt: As part of an effort to encourage a common language in threat actor analysis, CISA has released Best Practices for MITRE ATT&CK® Mapping . The guide shows analysts—through instructions and examples—how to map adversary behavior to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Excerpt: CISA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) have updated the joint cybersecurity advisory, Strengthening Cybersecurity of SATCOM Network Providers and Customers , originally released March 17, 2022, with U.S. government attribution to Russian state-sponsored malicious cyber actors . The United States assesses Russia launched cyberattacks in late February against commercial satellite communications networks to disrupt Ukrainian command and control during the Russia invasion, and those actions had spillover impacts into other European countries. CISA is working with both international and JCDC partners to strengthen our collective cybersecurity resilience—especially in the critical infrastructure that governments and citizens rely on—and to protect against and respond to malicious cyber activity. We continue to urge public and private sector partners to review and implement the guidance contained in U.S. government cybersecurity advisories, including Strengthening Cybersecurity of SATCOM Network Providers and Customer s, the January 2022 cybersecurity advisory on Protecting VSAT Communications , and the April 2022 cybersecurity advisory on Russian State-Sponsored and Criminal Threats to Critical Infrastructure . CISA also recommends partners review the CISA Shields Up , Shields Up Technical Guidance , and Russia webpages to stay current on the preventive measures that can help guard against Russian cyber threats and tactics.

Excerpt: CISA is temporarily removing CVE-2022-26925 from its Known Exploited Vulnerability Catalog due to a risk of authentication failures when the May 10, 2022 Microsoft rollup update is applied to domain controllers. After installing May 10, 2022 rollup update on domain controllers, organizations might experience authentication failures on the server or client for services, such as Network Policy Server (NPS), Routing and Remote access Service (RRAS), Radius, Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), and Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol (PEAP). Microsoft notified CISA of this issue, which is related to how the mapping of certificates to machine accounts is being handled by the domain controller. For more information see the Microsoft Knowledge Base article, KB5014754—Certificate-based authentication changes on Windows domain controllers: Key Distribution Center registry key . Note: installation of updates released May 10, 2022, on client Windows devices and non-domain controller Windows Servers will not cause this issue and is still strongly encouraged. This issue only affects May 10, 2022 updates installed on servers used as domain controllers. Organizations should continue to apply updates to client Windows devices and non-domain controller Windows Servers.
messages.output: A recent Microsoft update on domain controllers, specifically the May 10, 2022 rollup update, is causing authentication failures in various services. This issue is impacting Network Policy Server (NPS), Routing and Remote Access Service (RRAS), Radius, Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), and Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol (PEAP) functionalities. The vulnerability arises from the manner in which domain controllers handle certificate mapping to machine accounts. CISA has temporarily removed CVE-2022-26925 from its Known Exploited Vulnerability Catalog due to the risk associated with this update. For organizations running domain controllers, the May 10, 2022 update can lead to service disruptions and authentication issues. It's important to note that while the issue only affects domain controllers, client devices and non-domain controller servers are still recommended to be updated. To mitigate this risk, CISA advises that organizations apply the necessary updates to domain controllers only after understanding and addressing the potential impacts. For further details, refer to Microsoft’s KB5014754—Certificate-based authentication changes on Windows domain controllers: Key Distribution Center registry key.

Russian state-sponsored cyber operations frequently target critical infrastructure, particularly operational technology (OT) and industrial control systems (ICS) networks, with destructive malware. These state-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups have employed sophisticated cyber techniques to infiltrate U.S. and international critical infrastructure organizations, including those in the Defense Industrial Base, Healthcare and Public Health, Energy, Telecommunications, and Government Facilities sectors. The U.S. government has publicly attributed these activities to Russian state-sponsored APTs, including known campaigns that have used customized malware to compromise ICS networks.

According to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework, version 10, Russian state-sponsored APTs have commonly employed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) such as Credential Dumping, Living Off the Land, and Network Exploration. These tactics have been documented in various advisories and alerts, including information available on cisa.gov/Russia.

Given the evolving nature of Russian state-sponsored threats, it is crucial for critical infrastructure organizations to maintain resilience plans that address potential long-term disruptions in IT and OT environments. Organizations should implement robust mitigations as outlined by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the National Security Agency (NSA).

For OT assets, a key component of a resilience plan is ensuring that organizations can continue to operate even if they lose access to or control of their IT and OT systems. This can include maintaining offline backups, using air-gapped networks, and implementing segmented network architectures to minimize the impact of a potential cyber breach. Regularly updating and testing these resilience plans is essential to prepare for potential disruptions.

Russian state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) actors frequently leverage simple yet effective methods such as spearphishing, brute force attacks, and exploiting known vulnerabilities, especially in networks with weak security measures, to gain initial access to target networks. Known vulnerabilities that these actors have exploited include but are not limited to weak passwords, unpatched systems, and outdated software.

By following these recommendations, organizations can better defend against Russian state-sponsored APT actors and reduce the likelihood of severe business disruptions or data breaches.

On January 15, 2022, Microsoft unveiled a sophisticated malware campaign, named WhisperGate, that targeted numerous Ukrainian organizations. This malware operates in two stages: first, it corrupts the master boot record (MBR), then it displays a fake ransomware note before encrypting specific file types. Notably, even if a ransom is paid, the encrypted data cannot be recovered, as the malware actually destroys the targeted files. This information was further detailed in Microsoft’s blog post on destructive malware attacks against Ukrainian entities.

On February 23, 2022, cybersecurity researchers revealed the existence of a new malware variant, HermeticWiper, which has also been used against organizations in Ukraine. Excerpt: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA)—coauthored by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the Department of Energy (DOE)—provides information on multiple intrusion campaigns conducted by state-sponsored Russian cyber actors from 2011 to 2018 and targeted U.S. and international Energy Sector organizations. CISA, the FBI, and DOE responded to these campaigns with appropriate action in and around the time that they occurred. CISA, the FBI, and DOE are sharing this information in order to highlight historical tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used by adversaries to target U.S. and international Energy Sector organizations. On March 24, 2022, the U.S. Department of Justice unsealed indictments of three Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) officers and a Russian Federation Central Scientific Research Institute of Chemistry and Mechanics (TsNIIKhM) employee for their involvement in the following intrusion campaigns against U.S. and international oil refineries, nuclear facilities, and energy companies. This CSA provides the TTPs used by indicted FSB and TsNIIKhM actors in cyber operations against the global Energy Sector. Specifically, this advisory maps TTPs used in the global Energy Sector campaign and the compromise of the Middle East-based Energy Sector organization to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise and ATT&CK for ICS frameworks. CISA, the FBI, and DOE assess that state-sponsored Russian cyber operations continue to pose a threat to U.S. Energy Sector networks. CISA, the FBI, and DOE urge the Energy Sector and other critical infrastructure organizations to apply the recommendations listed in the Mitigations section of this advisory and Appendix A to reduce the risk of compromise. For more information on Russian state-sponsored malicious cyber activity, see CISA's Russia Cyber Threat Overview and Advisories webpage. For more information on the threat of Russian state-sponsored malicious cyber actors to U.S. critical infrastructure as well as additional mitigation recommendations, see joint CSA Understanding and Mitigating Russian State-Sponsored Cyber Threats to U.S. Critical Infrastructure and CISA's Shields Up Technical Guidance webpage.

These campaigns were meticulously carried out to compromise critical infrastructure, including oil refineries, nuclear facilities, and energy companies. In response to these threats, CISA, the FBI, and DOE took appropriate measures to mitigate the risks and share intelligence during and after the incidents.

Excerpt: Havex is a remote access Trojan (RAT) that communicates with a command and control (C2) server. The C2 server deploys payloads that enumerate all collected network resources and uses the Open Platform Communications (OPC) standard to gather information about connected control systems devices and resources within the network. Havex allowed the actor to install additional malware and extract data, including system information, lists of files and installed programs, e-mail address books, and virtual private network (VPN) configuration files. The Havex payload can cause common OPC platforms to crash, which could cause a denial-of-service condition on applications that rely on OPC communications. Note: for additional information on Havex, see to CISA ICS Advisory ICS Focused Malware and CISA ICS Alert ICS Focused Malware (Update A) . Beginning in 2016, the threat actor began widely targeting U.S. Energy Sector networks. The actor conducted these attacks in two stages: first targeting third-party commercial organizations (such as vendors, integrators, and suppliers) and then targeting Energy Sector organizations. The threat actor used the compromised third-party infrastructure to conduct spearphishing, watering hole, and supply chain attacks to harvest Energy Sector credentials and to pivot to Energy Sector enterprise networks. After obtaining access to the U.S. Energy Sector networks, the actor conducted network discovery, moved laterally, gained persistence, then collected and exfiltrated information pertaining to ICS from the enterprise, and possibly operational technology (OT), environments. Exfiltrated information included: vendor information, reference documents, ICS architecture, and layout diagrams. For more detailed information on FSB targeting of U.S. Energy Sector networks, See CISA Alert Russian Government Cyber Activity Targeting Energy Sector and Other Critical Infrastructure Sectors . Refer to Appendix A for TTPs of Havex malware and TTPs used by the actor in the 2016 to 2018 targeting of U.S. Energy Sector networks, as well as associated mitigations. In 2017, Russian cyber actors with ties to TsNIIKhM gained access to and manipulated a foreign oil refinery’s safety devices. TsNIIKhM actors used TRITON malware on the ICS controllers, which resulted in the refinery shutting down for several days.

Havex is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that operates by communicating with a command and control (C2) server. This C2 server deploys payloads designed to gather extensive network information. Havex specifically targets control systems using the Open Platform Communications (OPC) standard, enabling the actor to gather detailed information about connected devices and resources. Additionally, the malware can install further malware and extract data, such as system information, file lists, installed programs, email address books, and even virtual private network (VPN) configurations.

The Havex payload can induce OPC platforms to crash, potentially causing a denial-of-service condition in applications that rely on OPC communications. This capability allows the actor to disrupt critical operations without direct user interaction.

Beginning in 2016, Russian cyber actors associated with Havex targeted U.S. Energy Sector networks in a two-stage campaign. Initially, they compromised third-party commercial organizations, including vendors, integrators, and suppliers, to gain footholds. From there, they advanced to target Energy Sector organizations, using phishing and supply chain attacks to harvest credentials and pivot to the enterprise networks. Once inside, the actors conducted network discovery, lateral movement, and persistence establishment. They then collected and exfiltrated sensitive information, including vendor details, reference documents, ICS architecture, and layout diagrams.

In a notable incident in 2017, Russian cyber actors linked to TsNIIKhM gained unauthorized access to a foreign oil refinery’s safety devices. They deployed TRITON malware on the ICS controllers, leading to a significant shutdown of the refinery for several days. This incident underscores the potential for Havex and similar malware to cause severe operational disruptions.

For more detailed information on the Havex threat, refer to the CISA ICS Advisory on Focused Malware and CISA ICS Alert on Focused Malware (Update A). Additional insights can be found in CISA Alert on Russian Government Cyber Activity Targeting the Energy Sector and Other Critical Infrastructure Sectors. Appendix A provides TTPs of Havex and the tactics used by the actors, along with associated mitigation strategies.

Excerpt: March 9, 2022: this joint CSA was updated to include indicators of compromise (see below) and the United States Secret Service as a co-author. Notable attack vectors include Trickbot and Cobalt Strike (see below for details). While there are no specific or credible cyber threats to the U.S. homeland at this time, CISA, FBI, and NSA encourage organizations to review this advisory and apply the recommended mitigations. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) have observed the increased use of Conti ransomware in more than 400 attacks on U.S. and international organizations. (See FBI Flash: Conti Ransomware Attacks Impact Healthcare and First Responder Networks .) In typical Conti ransomware attacks, malicious cyber actors steal files, encrypt servers and workstations, and demand a ransom payment. To secure systems against Conti ransomware, CISA, FBI, and the National Security Agency (NSA) recommend implementing the mitigation measures described in this Advisory, which include requiring multifactor authentication (MFA), implementing network segmentation, and keeping operating systems and software up to date. Note: This Alert uses the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK®) framework, version 9. See the ATT&CK for Enterprise for all referenced threat actor tactics and techniques. While Conti is considered a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) model ransomware variant, there is variation in its structure that differentiates it from a typical affiliate model. It is likely that Conti developers pay the deployers of the ransomware a wage rather than a percentage of the proceeds used by affiliate cyber actors and receives a share of the proceeds from a successful attack.

Excerpt: In the execution phase [ TA0002 ], actors run a payload before using a more aggressive payload to reduce the risk of triggering antivirus engines. CISA and FBI have observed Conti actors using Router Scan, a penetration testing tool, to maliciously scan for and brute force [ T1110 ] routers, cameras, and network-attached storage devices with web interfaces. Additionally, actors use Kerberos attacks [ T1558.003 ] to attempt to get the Admin hash to conduct brute force attacks. Conti actors are known to exploit legitimate remote monitoring and management software and remote desktop software as backdoors to maintain persistence [ TA0003 ] on victim networks. The actors use tools already available on the victim network—and, as needed, add additional tools, such as Windows Sysinternals and Mimikatz—to obtain users’ hashes and clear-text credentials, which enable the actors to escalate privileges [ TA0004 ] within a domain and perform other post-exploitation and lateral movement tasks [ TA0008 ]. In some cases, the actors also use TrickBot malware to carry out post-exploitation tasks. Artifacts leaked with the playbook identify four Cobalt Strike server Internet Protocol (IP) addresses Conti actors previously used to communicate with their command and control (C2) server. Conti actors often use the open-source Rclone command line program for data exfiltration [ TA0010 ]. After the actors steal and encrypt the victim's sensitive data [ T1486 ], they employ a double extortion technique in which they demand the victim pay a ransom for the release of the encrypted data and threaten the victim with public release of the data if the ransom is not paid. Updated March 9, 2022: The following domains have registration and naming characteristics similar to domains used by groups that have distributed Conti ransomware. Many of these domains have been used in malicious operations; however, some may be abandoned or may share similar characteristics coincidentally. CISA, FBI, and NSA recommend that network defenders apply the following mitigations to reduce the risk of compromise by Conti ransomware attacks. Review CISA’s APTs Targeting IT Service Provider Customers guidance for additional mitigations specific to IT Service Providers and their customers.
messages.output:
In the execution phase, threat actors associated with the Conti ransomware group employ a sophisticated multi-layered approach to minimize the risk of detection by antivirus solutions. They initiate their operations by deploying a less aggressive payload, which serves as a probe to gain initial access, before escalating to more potent malware. The group has been observed using a penetration testing tool called Router Scan to systematically identify and brute-force routers, network-attached storage (NAS) devices, and cameras that have web interfaces, thereby gaining footholds into their targets' networks.

In addition to the brute-force attacks, the Conti actors utilize Kerberos attacks, specifically targeting the Admin hash, to facilitate further network penetration. These attacks enable the actors to conduct more aggressive brute-force attempts and to maintain persistent access to the victim's systems. The group is known for exploiting legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software and remote desktop protocols (RDP) to establish backdoors that allow them to remain undetected within the network. They often leverage tools already present on the victim's network, such as Windows Sysinternals and Mimikatz, to extract users' hashes and clear-text credentials. This information is crucial for privilege escalation within the domain and for performing post-exploitation tasks, including lateral movement to other parts of the network.

In some instances, the Conti actors deploy TrickBot malware to carry out post-exploitation operations. This malware provides a versatile framework for executing a wide range of tasks, including credential theft and data exfiltration. The group has been linked to four specific Cobalt Strike server IP addresses, which they use to communicate with their command and control (C2) infrastructure. For data exfiltration, the actors frequently employ the open-source Rclone command line program, which facilitates the transfer of sensitive data from the victim's network to the attackers.

Once the actors have encrypted the victim's sensitive data, they employ a double extortion tactic, demanding ransom payments in exchange for the decryption keys. If the ransom is not paid, the attackers threaten to publicly release the stolen data, thereby maximizing their leverage over the victim. This approach has proven highly effective, as evidenced by the frequency with which victims succumb to these threats.

To mitigate the risk of Conti ransomware attacks, network defenders are advised to implement the following measures: regularly update and patch systems, limit administrative privileges, monitor network traffic for unusual activity, and implement robust data backup and recovery procedures. These recommendations, along with CISA’s guidance for IT service providers and their customers, can significantly reduce the risk of compromise by Conti and similar threat actors.

If the ransom is not paid, the attackers threaten to publicly release the stolen data, thereby maximizing their leverage over the victim. Excerpt: On August 17, 2021, BlackBerry publicly disclosed that its QNX Real Time Operating System (RTOS) is affected by a BadAlloc vulnerability—CVE-2021-22156. BadAlloc is a collection of vulnerabilities affecting multiple RTOSs and supporting libraries. A remote attacker could exploit CVE-2021-22156 to cause a denial-of-service condition or execute arbitrary code on affected devices. BlackBerry QNX RTOS is used in a wide range of products whose compromise could result in a malicious actor gaining control of highly sensitive systems, increasing risk to the Nation’s critical functions. Note : at this time, CISA is not aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability. CISA strongly encourages critical infrastructure organizations and other organization developing, maintaining, supporting, or using affected QNX-based systems, to patch affected products as quickly as possible. Refer to the Mitigations section for more information about patching. CVE-2021-22156 is an integer overflow vulnerability affecting the function in the C runtime library of multiple BlackBerry QNX products. Exploitation of this vulnerability could lead to a denial-of-service condition or arbitrary code execution in affected devices. To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker must have control over the parameters to a function call and the ability to control what memory is accessed after the allocation. An attacker with network access could remotely exploit this vulnerability if the vulnerable product is running and the affected device is exposed to the internet. CVE-2021-22156 is part of a collection of integer overflow vulnerabilities, known as BadAlloc, which affect a wide range of industries using Internet of Things (IoT), and operational technology (OT)/industrial control systems (ICS) devices. See CISA ICS Advisory ICSA-21-119-04 and Microsoft’s BadAlloc blog post for more information. All BlackBerry programs with dependency on the C runtime library are affected by this vulnerability (see table 1 for a list of affected BlackBerry QNX products). Because many affected devices include safety-critical devices, exploitation of this vulnerability could result in a malicious actor gaining control of sensitive systems, possibly leading to increased risk of damage to infrastructure or critical functions.

Excerpt: This Joint Cybersecurity Advisory was written by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to provide information on a Chinese Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) group known in open-source reporting as APT40. This advisory provides APT40’s tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help cybersecurity practitioners identify and remediate APT40 intrusions and established footholds. On July 19, 2021, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) unsealed an indictment against four APT40 cyber actors for their illicit computer network exploitation (CNE) activities via front company Hainan Xiandun Technology Development Company (Hainan Xiandun). Hainan Xiandun employee Wu Shurong cooperated with and carried out orders from PRC Ministry of State Security (MSS) Hainan State Security Department (HSSD) intelligence officers Ding Xiaoyang, Zhu Yunmin, and Cheng Qingmin to conduct CNE. Wu’s CNE activities resulted in the theft of trade secrets, intellectual property, and other high-value information from companies and organizations in the United States and abroad, as well as from multiple foreign governments. These MSS-affiliated actors targeted victims in the following industries: academia, aerospace/aviation, biomedical, defense industrial base, education, government, healthcare, manufacturing, maritime, research institutes, and transportation (rail and shipping). Click here for indicators of compromise (IOCs) in STIX format. Note: to uncover malicious activity, incident responders search for IOCs in network- and host-based artifacts and assess the results—eliminating false positives during the assessment. For example, some MD5 IOCs in the STIX file identify legitimate tools—such as Putty, cmd.exe, svchost.exe, etc.—as indicators of compromise. Although the tools themselves are not malicious, APT40 attackers placed and used them from non-standard folders on victim systems during computer intrusion activity. If a legitimate tool is identified by an incident responder, then the location of the tool should be assessed to eliminate false positives or to uncover malicious activity. See Technical Approaches to Uncovering and Remediating Malicious Activity for more incident handling guidance. This Joint Cybersecurity Advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK® framework, version 9. See the ATT&CK for Enterprise framework for all referenced threat actor tactics and techniques.

This joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA)—authored by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and National Security Agency (NSA)—is part of our continuing cybersecurity mission to warn organizations of cyber threats and help the cybersecurity community reduce the risk presented by these threats. Threat intelligence analysis for critical infrastructure organizations should focus on immediate and comprehensive cybersecurity measures to enhance their posture against potential Russian state-sponsored cyber threats. Organizations must prioritize the patching of all systems, specifically focusing on known exploited vulnerabilities. Implementing multi-factor authentication (MFA) is essential to prevent unauthorized access. Additionally, the deployment of robust antivirus software can help mitigate threats from malware.

It is also crucial for organizations to develop and maintain internal contact lists for surge support in case of a cyber incident. This proactive approach ensures that there are immediate and coordinated responses to potential security breaches.

This advisory is part of a joint effort by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the National Security Agency (NSA). These agencies leverage the MITRE ATT&CK framework, version 10, to identify and warn about Russian state-sponsored cyber operations and their tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

Historically, Russian state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) actors have employed common yet effective methods such as spear-phishing, brute-force attacks, and exploiting known vulnerabilities to gain initial access to target networks. They have also demonstrated the ability to exploit third-party infrastructure and software, and they deploy custom malware.

Moreover, these APT actors can maintain persistent, undetected access for long periods, including in cloud environments, by leveraging legitimate credentials. This ability underscores the need for organizations to adopt heightened cybersecurity measures and conduct proactive threat hunting.

CISA, the FBI, and NSA strongly recommend implementing the following mitigations to improve functional resilience and reduce the risk of compromise or severe business disruption:

1. **Patch Management**: Prioritize patching known vulnerabilities.
2. **Multi-Factor Authentication**: Ensure that all critical access points are protected with MFA.
3. **Antivirus Deployment**: Install and maintain up-to-date antivirus software.
4. **Internal Contact Lists**: Establish and maintain communication channels for rapid response and support.
5. **Proactive Threat Hunting**: Regularly conduct proactive threat hunting to detect and mitigate threats.

Organizations are encouraged to review CISA Insights: Preparing for and Mitigating Cyber Threats for additional guidance on reducing cyber risks specific to their operations. By taking these steps, critical infrastructure organizations can significantly enhance their cybersecurity posture against Russian state-sponsored threats.

Excerpt: This advisory defines MSPs as entities that deliver, operate, or manage ICT services and functions for their customers via a contractual arrangement, such as a service level agreement. In addition to offering their own services, an MSP may offer services in conjunction with those of other providers. Offerings may include platform, software, and IT infrastructure services; business process and support functions; and cybersecurity services. MSPs typically manage these services and functions in their customer's network environment—either on the customer's premises or hosted in the MSP's data center. Note: this advisory does not address guidance on cloud service providers (CSPs)—providers who handle the ICT needs of their customers via cloud services such as Software-as-a-Service, Platform-as-a-Service, and Infrastructure-as-a-Service; however, MSPs may offer these services as well. (See Appendix for additional definitions.) MSPs provide services that usually require both trusted network connectivity and privileged access to and from customer systems. Many organizations—ranging from large critical infrastructure organizations to small- and mid-sized businesses—use MSPs to manage ICT systems, store data, or support sensitive processes. Many organizations make use of MSPs to scale and support network environments and processes without expanding their internal staff or having to develop the capabilities internally. Whether the customer's network environment is on premises or externally hosted, threat actors can use a vulnerable MSP as an initial access vector to multiple victim networks, with globally cascading effects. The UK, Australian, Canadian, New Zealand, and U.S. cybersecurity authorities expect malicious cyber actors—including state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) groups—to step up their targeting of MSPs in their efforts to exploit provider-customer network trust relationships. For example, threat actors successfully compromising an MSP could enable follow-on activity—such as ransomware and cyber espionage—against the MSP as well as across the MSP's customer base.

This advisory highlights the critical role of Managed Service Providers (MSPs) in the delivery and management of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) services for their customers. MSPs offer a range of services, including platform, software, and IT infrastructure management, business process support, and cybersecurity services. These services can be hosted on the customer's premises or in the MSP's data center, providing a seamless and efficient solution for organizations of all sizes. While the advisory does not specifically address Cloud Service Providers (CSPs), it notes that many MSPs also offer cloud services like Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS), and Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS).

MSPs are trusted partners for organizations that require both technical expertise and trusted network connectivity. They enable businesses to scale their network environments and support sensitive processes without the need for significant internal staff or internal development of capabilities. However, this trust can be exploited by malicious actors, including state-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups, which are increasingly targeting MSPs.

A successful compromise of an MSP can serve as a gateway for cyber threats to multiple victim networks, leading to a wide range of malicious activities. These activities can include ransomware attacks and cyber espionage, potentially affecting not just the MSP itself but also its entire customer base. The UK, Australian, Canadian, New Zealand, and U.S. cybersecurity authorities warn that this trend is likely to continue, emphasizing the importance of robust security measures to protect MSPs and their customers from potential cyber threats.

These services can be hosted on the customer's premises or in the MSP's data center, providing a seamless and efficient solution for organizations of all sizes. While the advisory does not specifically address Cloud Service Providers (CSPs), it notes that many MSPs also offer cloud services like Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS), and Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS).

MSPs are trusted partners for organizations that require both technical expertise and trusted network connectivity. They enable businesses to scale their network environments and support sensitive processes without the need for significant internal staff or internal development of capabilities. However, this trust can be exploited by malicious actors, including state-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups, which are increasingly targeting MSPs.

A successful compromise of an MSP can serve as a gateway for cyber threats to multiple victim networks, leading to a wide range of malicious activities. These activities can include ransomware attacks and cyber espionage, potentially affecting not just the MSP itself but also its entire customer base. The UK, Australian, Canadian, New Zealand, and U.S. cybersecurity authorities warn that this trend is likely to continue, emphasizing the importance of robust security measures to protect MSPs and their customers from potential cyber threats.

The United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the United States have recently issued specific guidance aimed at managed service providers (MSPs) and their clients. This guidance is designed to facilitate transparent and well-informed discussions focused on securing sensitive data and information. The aim is to re-evaluate security processes and contractual commitments to align with the varying risk tolerances of each party, thereby reducing overall risk for both MSPs and their clients, as well as the global information and communication technology (ICT) community.

The cybersecurity authorities recommend that both MSPs and their clients implement a set of baseline security measures and operational controls. Clients should ensure that their service level agreements (SLAs) or contracts explicitly mandate the implementation of these measures and controls. The guidance also emphasizes that malicious cyber actors often exploit vulnerable devices and internet-facing services, conduct brute force attacks, and use phishing tactics. To mitigate these threats, MSPs and their clients should take proactive steps.

Useful resources for mitigating initial compromise attack methods include detailed guides and best practices. For instance, organizations are advised to store critical logs for at least six months to enhance detection capabilities. This can be achieved through a comprehensive security information and event management (SIEM) solution or discrete logging tools. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) in the UK provides guidance on the appropriate data to collect for security purposes and the timing of its use.

Furthermore, organizations should implement endpoint detection and network defense monitoring, as well as application allowlisting or denylisting, to bolster their security posture. Securing remote access applications and enforcing multi-factor authentication (MFA) where feasible are also critical. It's worth noting that recent actions by Russian state-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actors have highlighted vulnerabilities in MFA protocols, particularly the risk of "fail open" and re-enrollment scenarios. Therefore, organizations should review their MFA configuration policies to ensure robust protection against such threats.

In summary, the cybersecurity authorities' guidance underscores the importance of proactive security measures and clear contractual commitments between MSPs and their clients to effectively secure sensitive information and data.

Excerpt: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and the Department of the Treasury (Treasury) are releasing this joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) to provide information on Maui ransomware, which has been used by North Korean state-sponsored cyber actors since at least May 2021 to target Healthcare and Public Health (HPH) Sector organizations. This joint CSA provides information—including tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs)—on Maui ransomware obtained from FBI incident response activities and industry analysis of a Maui sample. The FBI, CISA, and Treasury urge HPH Sector organizations as well as other critical infrastructure organizations to apply the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this CSA to reduce the likelihood of compromise from ransomware operations. Victims of Maui ransomware should report the incident to their local FBI field office or CISA. The FBI, CISA, and Treasury highly discourage paying ransoms as doing so does not guarantee files and records will be recovered and may pose sanctions risks. Note: in September 2021, Treasury issued an updated advisory highlighting the sanctions risks associated with ransomware payments and the proactive steps companies can take to mitigate such risks. Specifically, the updated advisory encourages U.S. entities to adopt and improve cybersecurity practices and report ransomware attacks to, and fully cooperate with, law enforcement. The updated advisory states that when affected parties take these proactive steps, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) would be more likely to resolve apparent sanctions violations involving ransomware attacks with a non-public enforcement response. For more information on state-sponsored North Korean malicious cyber activity, see CISA’s North Korea Cyber Threat Overview and Advisories webpage. Since May 2021, the FBI has observed and responded to multiple Maui ransomware incidents at HPH Sector organizations. North Korean state-sponsored cyber actors used Maui ransomware in these incidents to encrypt servers responsible for healthcare services—including electronic health records services, diagnostics services, imaging services, and intranet services. In some cases, these incidents disrupted the services provided by the targeted HPH Sector organizations for prolonged periods. The initial access vector(s) for these incidents is unknown.

The FBI, CISA, and the Department of the Treasury have collaborated to issue a joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) on Maui ransomware, a tool employed by North Korean state-sponsored cyber actors since May 2021. The advisory provides a detailed analysis of Maui ransomware, including its tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs), derived from FBI incident response activities and industry analysis. This advisory is aimed at Healthcare and Public Health (HPH) Sector organizations, as well as other critical infrastructure entities, to enhance their cybersecurity posture and mitigate risks.

Victims of Maui ransomware are advised to report the incident to their local FBI field office or CISA. The agencies strongly discourage paying ransoms, as this approach has no guarantee of file recovery and may result in sanctions risks. In September 2021, the Department of the Treasury issued an updated advisory emphasizing the sanctions implications of ransomware payments. It encourages U.S. entities to bolster their cybersecurity practices and to fully cooperate with law enforcement when reporting ransomware attacks. When these proactive measures are taken, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is more likely to resolve potential sanctions violations through non-public enforcement responses.

The FBI's incident response efforts have uncovered multiple cases of Maui ransomware affecting HPH Sector organizations since May 2021. The North Korean state-sponsored actors utilized Maui to encrypt servers critical for healthcare services, such as electronic health records, diagnostics, imaging, and intranet services. These incidents have led to prolonged service disruptions at targeted organizations. The initial access methods used by the attackers remain undisclosed, making prevention and mitigation efforts even more challenging.

Given the ongoing threat posed by North Korean state-sponsored cyber actors, the FBI, CISA, and the Department of the Treasury recommend that all organizations in the HPH Sector and critical infrastructure take proactive measures to strengthen their cybersecurity defenses. This includes applying the recommendations detailed in the CSA to reduce the risk of ransomware attacks and ensure continuity of operations.

### Cyber Threat Intelligence Report

This Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) is a collaborative effort among the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the National Security Agency (NSA), U.S. Cyber Command (USCC) - Cyber National Mission Force (CNMF), the Department of the Treasury (Treasury), the Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC), the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS), and the United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC). The authors are collectively identifying ongoing malicious cyber activities by advanced persistent threat (APT) actors, which they assess are linked to the Iranian Government’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The IRGC is an Iranian Government agency tasked with defending the Iranian Regime from both internal and external threats.

This advisory builds upon the previous joint CSA highlighting Iranian government-sponsored APT actors who exploited vulnerabilities in Microsoft Exchange and Fortinet software to gain initial access to targeted entities. The authoring agencies now categorize these actors as an APT group affiliated with the IRGC. Since the initial report in the FBI's Liaison Alert System (FLASH) from May 2021, the agencies have observed sustained and evolving activities from these IRGC-affiliated actors, including the exploitation of VMware Horizon Log4j vulnerabilities.

The actors' tactics involve gaining initial access to systems through these vulnerabilities and then using this foothold to conduct follow-on activities, such as disk encryption and data extortion, which support ransom operations. These activities underscore the importance of maintaining robust cybersecurity measures.

To protect against these threats, organizations are advised to take the following actions:

1. **Keep Systems and Software Updated:** Regularly patch and update systems to address known vulnerabilities. Prioritize remediation of known exploited vulnerabilities to mitigate risks.
2. **Implement Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):** Enforce the use of MFA to add an extra layer of security and prevent unauthorized access.
3. **Regularly Back Up Data:** Make offline backups of critical data to ensure that you can recover operations quickly if a ransomware attack occurs.

This advisory aims to provide timely and actionable information to help organizations defend against ransomware operations and related malicious activities.

Recent threat intelligence indicates that Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)-affiliated actors are intensively targeting a wide array of entities, including those in the U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, as well as organizations in Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom. These actors often operate under the guise of Najee Technology Hooshmand Fater LLC, based in Karaj, Iran, and Afkar System Yazd Company, located in Yazd, Iran. The observed tactics, techniques, and indicators of compromise (IOCs) strongly suggest that these APT actors are exploiting known vulnerabilities on unprotected networks, rather than targeting specific entities or sectors.

The authoring agencies have identified a pattern of behavior where these actors have been scanning for and exploiting several known vulnerabilities, including CVE-2018-13379, CVE-2020-12812, CVE-2019-5591, and CVE-2021-34473 (a ProxyShell vulnerability), since early 2021. These vulnerabilities have been used to gain initial access to a broad range of targeted entities. In particular, the authoring agencies have noted the exploitation of CVE-2021-34473 in conjunction with ProxyShell vulnerabilities CVE-2021-34523 and CVE-2021-31207, especially on U.S. networks.

Notably, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has observed that Afkar System Yazd Company, based in Yazd, Iran, is actively targeting organizations in the United Kingdom. Additionally, the Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) has reported that these APT actors have used CVE-2021-34473 to gain access to systems within Australia. Once access is gained, these actors can deploy tools for ransom and extortion operations, as well as for data exfiltration.

Organizations, especially those in critical infrastructure, are urged to apply the recommended mitigations provided in the advisory to reduce the risk of compromise. For more information on Iranian state-sponsored malicious cyber activity, refer to CISA’s Iran Cyber Threat Overview and Advisories webpage and the FBI’s Iran Threat webpage.

Excerpt: Since the activity was reported in 2021, these IRGC-affiliated actors have continued to exploit known vulnerabilities for initial access. In addition to exploiting Fortinet and Microsoft Exchange vulnerabilities, the authoring agencies have observed these APT actors exploiting VMware Horizon Log4j vulnerabilities CVE-2021-44228 (“Log4Shell”), CVE-2021-45046 , and CVE-2021-45105 for initial access. The IRGC-affiliated actors have used their access for ransom operations, including disk encryption and extortion efforts. After gaining access to a network, the IRGC-affiliated actors likely determine a course of action based on their perceived value of the data. Depending on the perceived value, the actors may encrypt data for ransom and/or exfiltrate data. The actors may sell the data or use the exfiltrated data in extortion operations or “double extortion” ransom operations where a threat actor uses a combination of encryption and data theft to pressure targeted entities to pay ransom demands. Note : This advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework, version 11. See Appendix B for a table of the MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques observed. The IRGC-affiliated actors have used the following malicious and legitimate tools [ T1588.001 , T1588.002 ] for a variety of tactics across the enterprise spectrum: Note : For additional tools used by these IRGC-affiliated cyber actors, see joint CSA Iranian Government-Sponsored APT Cyber Actors Exploiting Microsoft Exchange and Fortinet Vulnerabilities in Furtherance of Malicious Activities . As stated in the Technical Details section previously reported in joint CSA Iranian Government-Sponsored APT Cyber Actors Exploiting Microsoft Exchange and Fortinet Vulnerabilities in Furtherance of Malicious Activities , the IRGC-affiliated actors gained initial access by exploiting known vulnerabilities [ T1190 ]. The IRGC-affiliated actors may have made modifications to the Task Scheduler [ T1053.005 ]. These modifications may display as unrecognized scheduled tasks or actions. Specifically, the below established tasks may be associated with this activity: Note: The potential exists that tasks associated with CacheTask or Wininet may be legitimate. For additional tasks used by these IRGC-affiliated cyber actors, see joint CSA Iranian Government-Sponsored APT Cyber Actors Exploiting Microsoft Exchange and Fortinet Vulnerabilities in Furtherance of Malicious Activities .
messages.output:
Since the initial reports in 2021, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)-affiliated actors have continued to exploit known vulnerabilities for gaining initial access to networks. Their modus operandi includes exploiting vulnerabilities in Fortinet and Microsoft Exchange, as well as more recent vulnerabilities like VMware Horizon Log4j (CVE-2021-44228), CVE-2021-45046, and CVE-2021-45105. These actors have leveraged their access for ransomware operations, employing techniques such as disk encryption and data exfiltration. The nature of their actions is often determined by the perceived value of the targeted data. If the data is deemed valuable, the actors may encrypt it for ransom or exfiltrate it for sale or use in subsequent extortion efforts, including “double extortion” ransom attacks.

The attackers have employed a range of techniques and tools, including legitimate ones that can be repurposed for malicious use, such as those listed in the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework, version 11. Specifically, these actors have used malicious and legitimate tools (T1588.001 and T1588.002) across various tactics. The techniques observed include leveraging known vulnerabilities for initial access (T1190) and modifying the Task Scheduler (T1053.005), which can result in unrecognized or disguised scheduled tasks.

The Task Scheduler modifications may appear as unrecognized scheduled tasks, such as CacheTask or Wininet, potentially leading to confusion and undetected malicious activity. The use of these tools and techniques reflects the sophistication and persistent nature of these cyber threats, and highlights the continuous evolution of their tactics. For a more comprehensive list of tools and techniques used by these IRGC-affiliated actors, refer to the joint advisory from the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Iranian government-sponsored APT actors exploiting Microsoft Exchange and Fortinet vulnerabilities.

334 words that covers the same activity in your own words. Return only the text.
Excerpt: CISA is tracking a significant cyber incident impacting enterprise networks across federal, state, and local governments, as well as critical infrastructure entities and other private sector organizations. An advanced persistent threat (APT) actor is responsible for compromising the SolarWinds Orion software supply chain, as well as widespread abuse of commonly used authentication mechanisms. This threat actor has the resources, patience, and expertise to gain access to and privileges over highly sensitive information if left unchecked. CISA urges organizations to prioritize measures to identify and address this threat. Pursuant to Presidential Policy Directive (PPD) 41, CISA, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) have formed a Cyber Unified Coordination Group (UCG) to coordinate a whole-of-government response to this significant cyber incident. CISA also remains in regular contact with public and private sector stakeholders and international partners, providing technical assistance upon request, and making information and resources available to help those affected to recover quickly from incidents related to this campaign. CISA encourages individuals and organizations to refer to the resources below for additional information on this compromise. These resources provide information to help organizations detect and prevent this activity. CISA released the CISA Hunt and Incident Response Program (CHIRP), a forensics collection capability outlined in Activity Alert AA21-077A and available on CISA’s CHIRP GitHub repository . This capability was developed to assist network defenders with detecting advanced persistent threat (APT) activity related to the SolarWinds and Active Directory/M365 compromise. The initial release of CHIRP scans for signs of APT compromise within an on-premises environment to detect indicators of compromise (IOCs) associated with CISA Alerts AA20-352A and AA21-008A . On January 6, 2021, CISA Released Supplemental Guidance on Emergency Directive 21-01 that requires (1) agencies that ran affected versions conduct forensic analysis, (2) agencies that accept the risk of running SolarWinds Orion comply with certain hardening requirements, and (3) reporting by agency from department-level Chief Information Officers (CIOs) by Tuesday, January 19, and Monday, January 25, 2020.
messages.output:
CISA is monitoring a major cyber event that has affected numerous networks, including those of federal, state, and local governments, critical infrastructure, and private sector entities. The incident involves an advanced persistent threat (APT) actor who has compromised the SolarWinds Orion software supply chain and has also misused common authentication mechanisms. This APT actor, known for its resourcefulness and persistence, poses a significant risk to sensitive information if not mitigated promptly. CISA advises organizations to take immediate action to identify and address this threat.

In response to this incident, CISA, along with the FBI and the ODNI, has established a Cyber Unified Coordination Group (UCG) to coordinate a whole-of-government response. This group aims to manage and mitigate the cyber threat efficiently. CISA is also in frequent communication with public and private sector stakeholders and international partners, offering technical support and resources to assist organizations in recovering from this incident.

To aid organizations in detecting and preventing this activity, CISA has developed the CISA Hunt and Incident Response Program (CHIRP). CHIRP is a forensics collection capability detailed in Activity Alert AA21-077A, which is available on CISA’s CHIRP GitHub repository. This tool helps network defenders identify signs of APT compromise within their on-premises environments by scanning for indicators of compromise (IOCs) linked to CISA Alerts AA20-352A and AA21-008A.

On January 6, 2021, CISA issued Supplemental Guidance on Emergency Directive 21-01. This directive requires agencies that ran affected versions of the software to conduct forensic analysis, agencies that accept the risk of using the compromised SolarWinds Orion to comply with specific hardening requirements, and reporting from agency-level Chief Information Officers (CIOs) by January 19 and 25, 2021.

These measures underscore the severity of the threat and the critical need for organizations to take proactive steps to secure their networks and systems.
